title: The Money Changes Its Mind
author: The Work Forward
summary: In 'The Money Changes Its Mind,' a Work Forward essay draws on the author's own experience running a struggling ecommerce-to-SaaS holding company through the 2010s - eventually laying off staff across three offices to service debt - to argue that founders' outcomes are often set less by their decisions than by what their investors' capital needs. The piece contrasts that personal story with Airtable's 2026 sale to Bending Spoons: a disciplined exit that carved out the company's AI bet, returned cash to investors, and left the mature business to an operator built for it. It then surveys a pattern in recent AI 'acquihire' deals (Microsoft-Inflection, Google-Character.AI, Google-Windsurf) where founders and top researchers land generational paydays while most employees are left holding equity that has effectively been zeroed out, unless a buyer chooses to waive vesting cliffs. The essay's takeaway for leaders and founders is that 'the money will change its mind' regardless of how good the investors are, and offers three concrete defenses: build ownership-level control and governance before success attracts pressure, prioritize profitability so outside capital's clock isn't the only clock running, and tell your team plainly where they sit in the liquidation stack before they find out in a crisis.
points: The author's central lesson, learned running a struggling ecommerce-to-SaaS conglomerate in the 2010s, is that 'the box canyon we were driving into wasn't walled in by our decisions. It was walled in by what the money needed.'
Contrasting Airtable's disciplined $1.285 billion sale against his own 2010s forced fire-sale illustrates the difference between proactively managing 'financial gravity' and being dragged by it.

Recent AI 'acquihire' deals (Inflection, Character.AI, Windsurf) show a repeatable pattern: founders and top researchers get generational payouts while most employees are left holding vaporized equity, unless a buyer voluntarily waives vesting cliffs.

Three concrete defenses are offered: control the business at the ownership level before success attracts pressure, get profitable early so the fund's clock isn't yours, and tell your team the truth about where they sit in the equity stack before they learn it at the worst moment.
quotes: But the money had needs. Debt must be serviced, covenants untripped.

I own a big share of how all of that went. I could have pushed harder to move resources out of the legacy business and into the next one, cut heads faster, or gotten any of a hundred other calls right that I got wrong.
The box canyon we were driving into wasn't walled in by our decisions. It was walled in by what the money needed.
If your company is funded by anyone, venture, growth equity, private equity, a friendly billionaire, take one thing from these stories. The money will change its mind.

His term is "financial gravity," the pull that drags companies off their purpose as a structural inevitability, not a failure of character. The fix is governance you build before you're successful, because success is what attracts the pressure.
Get profitable as early as you can. Profitability is what lets you say no. Every month you can fund yourself is a month the fund's clock isn't yours.

Know where your people sit in the stack, and tell them the truth about it. If they're holding common under a mountain of preferences, they're further from a payout than your all-hands slides imply, and they'll learn it at the worst moment.
